title: Business Logic & Problem Solving
goal: Translate business requirements into clear, testable algorithms.

material.explanation: Turn a feature request into observable behavior before choosing classes. Separate stated rules from assumptions and unresolved questions. A requirement should identify an actor, an action, and an outcome you can verify.

topics.title: Preconditions
topics.description: Preconditions describe what must be true before an operation proceeds.
learningGoals: Rejections are explicit and repeatable
No state changes before a rejected precondition
examples: Cancel an order in PAID state.

tasks.title: Explain Preconditions in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Preconditions describe what must be true before an operation proceeds. State whether failure returns a result or raises a domain error. Check requirements at the boundary that owns them, and avoid changing state before all necessary checks pass.

workedExample.scenario: Cancel an order in PAID state.
steps: Verify it exists.
Reject the transition without modifying payment or order state.

commonMistakes: A failed precondition must not leave partial side effects.
material.independentExercise: Specify reservation preconditions for quantity and available stock.
recallQuestions: Which object owns each check?
What happens if multiple checks fail?

acceptanceCriteria: Rejections are explicit and repeatable
No state changes before a rejected precondition

topics.title: Postconditions
topics.description: Postconditions state what is true after completion.
learningGoals: Success satisfies every promised state change
Failure preserves documented invariants
examples: Refund 20 from an unrefunded payment of 100.

tasks.title: Explain Postconditions in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: Postconditions state what is true after completion. Describe successful state changes and what remains unchanged after failure. Include externally visible side effects so a returned success cannot hide incomplete work.

workedExample.scenario: Refund 20 from an unrefunded payment of 100.
steps: Refunded total becomes 20.
A rejected second request changes neither total nor audit state.

commonMistakes: Returning success does not prove all required state changes occurred.
guidedExercise: Write refund success and rejection postconditions
material.independentExercise: Define reservation postconditions for stock, reservation ID, and expiration.
recallQuestions: What must be true after success?
What must remain unchanged after failure?

acceptanceCriteria: Success satisfies every promised state change
Failure preserves documented invariants

topics.title: Invariants
topics.description: An invariant must hold for all publicly observable valid states.
learningGoals: All operations preserve the invariant
A competing-request example exposes the atomicity requirement
examples: A payment totals 100 and refunds total 80.

tasks.title: Explain Invariants in your own words
Work through the example and predict the result
Check a boundary or failure case without AI implementation help

material.explanation: An invariant must hold for all publicly observable valid states. Identify the state needed to enforce it and put the check with that owner. Multi-object invariants may require an atomic boundary rather than independent local checks.

workedExample.scenario: A payment totals 100 and refunds total 80.
steps: A new refund of 30 is rejected.
The refunded total never exceeds 100.

commonMistakes: Checking each request amount against the original payment ignores previous refunds.
material.independentExercise: Maintain available stock plus active reservations without negative quantities.
recallQuestions: When must an invariant hold?
Which state is needed to enforce it?

acceptanceCriteria: All operations preserve the invariant
A competing-request example exposes the atomicity requirement

steps: Load and validate it.

material.explanation: A failure path describes rejection or interruption at a specific step. Distinguish business rejection from infrastructure uncertainty. State whether prior work rolls back, remains committed, or requires recovery.

steps: Do not report a completed refund.

topics.title: Edge cases

tasks.title: Explain the idea in your own words

material.explanation: Edge cases arise at limits and unusual but valid combinations. Derive them from the rules: zero, maximum, empty, exact time, duplicates, and competing actions. Record expected results before running code.

steps: Test just before noon.

commonMistakes: Random tests alone may never exercise the exact boundary.

acceptanceCriteria: Boundary outcomes are decided before implementation

material.explanation: A transition moves a domain object between valid states under specified conditions. List allowed edges and terminal states. Under concurrency, checking and applying a transition must act as one protected decision.

steps: PAID and SHIPPED reject cancellation in this exercise.
CANCELLED rejects another cancellation.

acceptanceCriteria: Forbidden edges cannot mutate state
Repeated terminal actions follow a documented policy

tasks.title: Design processRefund(transactionId, amount)
Support partial refund
Prevent duplicate refund
Reject refund larger than remaining original amount
Check boundary and failure cases
Verify: Cumulative refunds never exceed the paid amount
Verify: Zero, negative, and excess amounts reject
Verify: Repeated keys create no second refund and changed payload conflicts
Verify: Concurrent and uncertain-outcome cases are specified

requirements: Design processRefund(transactionId, amount) with a separate request identity for retries
Amount is positive, currency-compatible, and no greater than the remaining refundable amount
Support multiple partial refunds whose total never exceeds the payment
Same request key and payload return the existing outcome; changed payload conflicts

material.explanation: A refund is constrained by previous refunds, not only the original charge. Include request identity and outcome retention in the contract so a lost response does not cause an accidental second effect. Separate provider uncertainty from definite rejection.

steps: A new 20 refund leaves 50 refundable.
Repeating its request key does not add another 20.

tasks.title: Verify: Stock conservation and nonnegative availability hold
Verify: Release and expiry cannot restore units twice
Verify: Expiration equality and competing terminal actions are specified
Verify: Duplicate requests have a precise policy

exercises.description: Transfer the same reasoning to stock reservation instead of authentication.
learningGoals: Transfer the same reasoning to stock reservation instead of authentication.
Demonstrate the acceptance criteria with observable evidence.
examples: Stock is five and a reservation requests two.
requirements: reserveStock(itemId, quantity, requestKey) reserves a positive quantity
Available stock must never become negative
Reservations start ACTIVE and can become CONFIRMED, RELEASED, or EXPIRED
Release and expiration restore reserved stock exactly once
Repeated request keys obey a stated payload and outcome policy
Expired reservations cannot be confirmed
constraints: Design first; use a controllable clock for any implementation
deliverables: Working solution or design, as specified

material.explanation: This exercise checks whether you can transfer invariants and lifecycle reasoning to a new domain. Identify how physical stock, active reservations, and available stock relate. Describe terminal actions and competing confirmation versus expiration.

workedExample.scenario: Stock is five and a reservation requests two.
steps: Available stock becomes three.
Release restores five once; a second release adds nothing.

commonMistakes: Do not treat a successful demonstration as proof of all rules. Explain rejection behavior and show state after failure.
guidedExercise: Trace expiration and confirmation at the same boundary.
material.independentExercise: Design two simultaneous reservations for the last item and identify the required atomic decision.
recallQuestions: What restores stock exactly once?
Which operation owns expiration versus confirmation?

acceptanceCriteria: Stock conservation and nonnegative availability hold
Release and expiry cannot restore units twice
Expiration equality and competing terminal actions are specified
Duplicate requests have a precise policy
